title: French opposition battles to rise from the rubble of Macron's win
text: Bruised and battered after their electoral defeat by Emmanuel Macron's centrists, France's Socialist Party is laying off most of its staff and selling its Paris base, while the centre-right Republicans limp along in search of a leader. With membership falling after it won just six percent of the vote in the presidential election, the centre-left party told staff on Wednesday that it would have to fire most of them, days after its historic headquarters was put up for sale to raise money. Across the political divide, the conservative Republicans have no leader and have spent months struggling to decide whether to expel party members who have signed up to serve with Macron. The two parties governed France for decades, but Macron's Republic on the Move has taken the middle ground from under their feet. Macron benefits from a large political space left vacant by the opposition, said Vincent Thibault of Elabe pollsters, adding that he faces very few attacks from the other parties. Because it has fewer lawmakers and local officials, the Socialist Party's income has dropped to 8 million euros ($9.42 million) a year from 28 million previously. Party treasurer Jean-Francois Debat told Reuters that around 60 of the 97 staff would have to go. The Republicans, although they are the largest opposition group in the lower house of parliament and hold a majority in the senate, are in barely better shape. For the past five months they have struggled to stop Macron from poaching their top officials, or to oppose economic policies that mirror their own. At the latest of several meetings on membership, the party decided in principle on Tuesday to expel Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and other ministers serving in Macron's government.

title: Aide to Macau billionaire in plea talks in U.N. bribery case
text: The assistant to a billionaire Macau real estate developer accused of taking part in a scheme to bribe a former United Nations General Assembly president is in plea talks, his lawyer said on Tuesday. The negotiations involving Jeff Yin, who was arrested together with billionaire Ng Lap Seng in 2015, were revealed in a letter his attorney filed in Manhattan federal court, which said prosecutors had extended him a plea offer. The lawyer, Sabrina Shroff, asked to extend court deadlines so that Yin, 31, could consider the offer, which “is complex and involves civil tax assessments and liabilities,” according to her letter. The talks come ahead of a jury trial scheduled for May 15, in which Yin and his boss could face substantial prison time if convicted. It was not clear what charges Yin would have to plead guilty to if he accepted. He had faced bribery, money laundering and tax-related charges, and was also accused of violating the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Shroff declined to comment. The U.S. Attorney's Office in Manhattan, which is pursuing the case, also declined to comment. Ng, who was once linked to a campaign fundraising investigation during former U.S. President Bill Clinton's administration, is one of seven people charged since October 2015 in the U.N.-related probe. Prosecutors accuse Ng and Yin of paying more than $500,000 in bribes to John Ashe, a former U.N. ambassador from Antigua and Barbuda who served as General Assembly president from 2013 to 2014. Ashe died in June while awaiting trial. According to the indictment, Ng and Yin also bribed Francis Lorenzo, then a deputy U.N. ambassador from the Dominican Republic, who pleaded guilty in March 2016 to bribery and money laundering charges as part of a deal to cooperate in the probe.

title: Trump set to sign cyber security executive order on Tuesday: sources
text: President Donald Trump is expected to sign an executive order on cyber security on Tuesday, according to two sources familiar with the matter, in what would be his first step to address an issue he has called a top priority of his administration. The order is expected to commission several separate reviews of the government's offensive and defensive cyber capabilities, according to one of those sources and a third person briefed on a draft of the order that circulated last week. It follows a presidential campaign dominated by running storylines about cyber security, including the hacking and later leaking of Democratic emails as part of what U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was a wide-ranging influence operation meant to help Trump win the White House and denigrate his Democratic challenger, Hillary Clinton. For months Trump refused to accept the agencies' conclusion that Russia was responsible, before saying at a press conference on January 11 that, “as far as hacking I think it was Russia.” In the same answer, Trump, then the president-elect, pivoted to say that “we also get hacked by other countries, and other people” while pledging a government-wide review of vulnerabilities to cyber attacks. The order is also expected to launch an audit of several federal agencies' cyber capabilities, seek input on how to better protect critical infrastructure, and review government efforts to attract and train a technically sophisticated workforce, according to two of the sources briefed on the draft, which was first published by the Washington Post. The draft order would also look for ways to give the private sector incentives to adopt strong security measures.

title: Funerals fill cemetery in Mexican city hit hardest by massive quake
text: Anguished mourners lined the streets of the southern Mexican city devastated by the most powerful earthquake to hit the country in 85 years, carrying coffins on their shoulders as they moved slowly toward a crowded cemetery on Saturday. More than half of the 65 known victims of Thursday night's magnitude 8.1 quake died in Juchitan, a picturesque, historic city near the coast where more than 5,000 homes were destroyed and many more were left without running water or electricity. In the Eighth Section neighborhood, a working-class district where almost every home was damaged, a loud drum and horn band played traditional music ahead of the funeral of one of the 37 dead recovered so far from the wreckage of the somber city. At times the piercing blasts of the burly horn section were drowned out by the plaintive wailing of mourners for Maximo Zuniga, a little boy who, his distraught relatives said, was fond of his spiky black hair and bright red tennis shoes. The three-year-old was asleep when the force of the quake sent the brick walls of his bedroom crumbling down on him, his mother and an older brother. The boy died soon after he was pulled from the rubble; the other two survived. I could barely see a little bit of his hair peeking out and his forehead, said neighbor Alejandro Sanchez, who was the first to come to the stricken family's aid. There was a heavy wooden beam on top of all three of them and lots of dirt, he added, as the dead boy's uncle sobbed uncontrollably nearby.

title: Bush's 2016 move pushes other potential GOP candidates into higher gear
text: Jeb Bush’s announcement this week that he is considering a 2016 presidential run appears to have opened the starting gate on the GOP primary, with other potential Republican hopefuls such as Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Dr. Ben Carson following with telltale moves of their own. Bush, a former Florida governor, said in a Facebook announcement on Tuesday that he is “actively” exploring a White House bid, and within hours Paul’s leadership political action committee followed with two Google ad buys. The first Rand PAC ad showed up in the search results of people who searched Bush’s name on Google. The second looked more like an attack ad, since it included the line “We need leaders who will stand against Common Core,” the national school-curriculum standards backed by Bush but opposed by conservative-minded supporters of state autonomy and less government. Later that night Paul, who says he is “still a few more months” away from a 2016 decision, said on Fox News’ “The Kelly File” that “Most of us believe in less federal government and more decentralized government, particularly with education. ... For Jeb Bush to run in the primary will be very, very difficult.” David Payne, a Republican strategist and a senior vice president at Washington, D.C.-based VOX Global, gave a mixed review of what he called the “digital shadow boxing,” and suggested GOP 2016 hopefuls will have to do more and do it better. “Facebook is a part of the established media landscape,” Payne told FoxNews.com. “Jeb Bush wasn’t breaking any new ground with his announcement on this platform. He’ll need to be a lot more innovative to get Republican primary voters interested in him.” He also said Paul’s counter punch was “intelligent but the expectation” from the relatively tech savvy Paul followers.

title: Meet The Upshot's Presidential Prediction Model
text: For now, at least, Hillary Clinton has a 76 percent chance of beating Donald Trump to become president of the United States. A Trump victory is still quite possible: Mrs. Clinton's chance of losing is roughly the same as the probability that an N.B.A. player will miss a free throw. This probability, the first forecast from the Upshot's presidential prediction model, is based on each state's voting history and on roughly 300 state and national polls of the race conducted to date. Our model suggests Mrs. Clinton is a strong favorite in 14 states and the District of Columbia, which would give her 186 of the 270 electoral votes she needs to win the White House. Add eight more states that polls currently show leaning Democratic, among them Minnesota, Michigan and Pennsylvania, and Mrs. Clinton would have 275 electoral votes and the presidency. But with 16 weeks left in the campaign, a lot can change. Using the same model, we would have given Bill Clinton less than a 20 percent chance of winning the presidency with about four months to go in 1992. His polls improved only after Ross Perot left the race and Democrats rallied around Mr. Clinton following the Democratic convention. And they improved sharply. A month later, he was an 84 percent favorite. Polling volatility of this kind should be expected, especially with the party conventions coming up. It is one reason Mrs. Clinton's probability of victory is not higher. Current polling averages point to Mrs. Clinton winning the national popular vote if nothing changes. But we expect changes between now and Election Day. The Upshot is not the only news organization trying to forecast the election results.

title: ‘Long and Genuine’ Hugs: Relatives of Shooting Victims Recall Obama’s Empathy
text: It was a wrenching ritual that has grown all too familiar to President Obama. He searches for words of sympathy, comfort and condolence and offers long, tight embraces that the mourners will remember far more vividly than anything he says.

title: Dam collapse fears deepen Puerto Rico's misery after hurricane
text: Puerto Rico's governor met mayors from across the ravaged island on Saturday after inspecting damage to an earthen dam in the northwestern part of the U.S. territory that was threatening to collapse from flooding in the wake of Hurricane Maria. Some 70,000 people living downstream from the compromised dam, which has formed a lake on the rain-swollen Guajataca River, were under orders to evacuate, with the structure at risk of bursting at any moment. We saw directly the damage to the Guajataca dam, Governor Ricardo Rossello said in a Spanish-language Twitter message on Saturday, repeating his request that people leave the area as soon as possible. The fissure has become a significant rupture, Rossello said separately at a news conference on Saturday. The U.S. National Weather Service said on its website that the dam was still in danger of failing and setting off life-threatening flash floods. Stay away or be swept away, it warned. Meanwhile, people across the island were struggling to dig out from the destruction left by the storm, which killed at least 25 people, including at least 10 in Puerto Rico, as it churned across the Caribbean, according to officials and media reports. To all Puerto Ricans, please know we will get back up, the governor tweeted as he met mayors in the territory to identify their most urgent needs. Together with the mayors, as one government. In a development that could aid the recovery effort, the Port of San Juan reopened, according to a Twitter message from the agency that runs it, allowing ships to unload supplies.

title: Senator Warren slams Equifax's potential to profit from data breach
text: U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized Equifax Inc on Wednesday, saying the company failed to adequately protect customers after a massive data breach and stood to profit from a hack that exposed information on more than 140 million people. “The breach of your system has actually created more business opportunities for you,” Warren, a Democrat known for her consumer advocacy, told former Equifax Chief Executive Officer Richard Smith during his second congressional grilling of the week. Besides providing consumer credit reports, Equifax sells products to protect people's data from misuse. Warren said this mix of businesses creates a conflict of interest, making Equifax responsible for protecting consumer data while allowing it to profit from consumers' efforts to mitigate the breach. “Equifax is making money, millions of dollars off its own screw-up and meanwhile the potential cost to Equifax are shockingly low,” Warren told Smith, 57, at the U.S. Senate Banking Committee hearing. Smith retired from the credit reporting company last week but was in charge during the breach, which the company disclosed last month. Smith acknowledged that the hack created an opportunity for fraud and that the company could profit from consumers trying to protect their data. But he defended Equifax's social utility. The company collects data on consumers and sells it to banks so they can better judge a borrower's creditworthiness. “The company has been around for 118 years and for most of those 118 years has done good things,” Smith said. After the hearing, Warren told reporters that Equifax's new product letting individuals “lock” and “unlock” their credit reports does not provide enough protection and that only a change in the law can fully shield people's information. “It only applies to Equifax.”

title: Trump to direct departments to strengthen cyber security
text: U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday put off signing an executive order expected to require the heads of government agencies to take a more direct role in reviewing and managing risks to the networks they control. Trump pledged that his administration will work with the private sector to make sure owners and operators of critical infrastructure have the support they need from the federal government to guard against cyber threats. Trump said he would take steps to ensure cyber security is central to the U.S. military.

title: Amazon Has Proved Infertile Ground for Unions, So Far
text: In early April, Kellen Wadach, the general manager of Amazon’s warehouse in Middletown, Del., told hundreds of workers at the cavernous facility a troubling story about how his father’s union had abandoned his family. Showing a photograph of himself as a boy with his father, Mr. Wadach said the union did not help his family financially after his father died suddenly in front of their house, and did not even bother to send a condolence card, according to three current workers at the warehouse who heard him speak and asked not to be named for fear of losing their jobs. The trouble with Mr. Wadach’s story was that much of it appears to have been untrue. For years, Amazon has successfully fought to keep unions out of the company. And the episode involving Mr. Wadach illustrated how important it was to Amazon, or at least to some of its employees, to keep things that way. Just days after a reporter asked Amazon about inconsistencies in Mr. Wadach’s story, Scott Stanzel, an Amazon spokesman, said Mr. Wadach no longer worked for the company. Mr. Wadach did not respond to repeated messages sent to his email address and Facebook account. A voice mail message left at a listed number for his mother was not returned. In the United States, Amazon employs more than 90,000 people in what it calls fulfillment centers, giant warehouses where customer orders are prepared and shipped. Some fulfillment center workers see unions as a way to gain more say over pay, how job assignments are handed out and how workplace complaints are handled. Amazon worries that unions will saddle its operations with red tape, hurting the nimbleness of facilities it is constantly adjusting to become more efficient with robots and other innovations.

Flashing a photograph of himself as a boy with his father, Mr. Wadach said the union did not help his family financially after his father died suddenly in front of their house, not even bothering to send a condolence card, according to three current workers at the warehouse who heard him speak and asked for anonymity for fear of losing their jobs. The problem with Mr. Wadach’s story was that much of it appears to have been untrue. For years, Amazon has relentlessly and successfully battled to keep unions out of the company. And the incident involving Mr. Wadach was a striking illustration of how important it was to Amazon, or at least to some of its employees, to keep it that way. Just days after a reporter approached Amazon about inconsistencies in Mr. Wadach’s story, Scott Stanzel, an Amazon spokesman, said Mr. Wadach was no longer with the company. Mr. Wadach did not respond to repeated messages sent to his email address and Facebook account. A voice mail message left at a listed number for his mother was not returned. In the United States, Amazon employs more than 90,000 people in what the company calls fulfillment centers, giant warehouses where customer orders are prepared and shipped. Some Amazon fulfillment center workers see unions as a way to gain more influence on pay, how job assignments are doled out and the handling of workplace complaints. Amazon worries unions will bury its operations in red tape, hurting the nimbleness of facilities it is constantly adjusting to be more efficient with robots and other innovations.

title: Trump defends his attacks on Mexican-American federal judge
text: Presumptive Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump on Friday defended his attacks on a Mexican-American judge, resisting pressure from top Republicans to tone down his rhetoric amid concern that he is damaging his chances of winning the White House. Trump's bomb-throwing rhetoric helped him beat 16 Republican rivals for the party's nomination for the Nov. 8 election. But with a tough fight ahead against expected Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton, many Republicans want him to project a more disciplined image. Confident that his approach has been a winner, Trump has so far brushed off some of the advice from Republicans who back him but want less loose talk. In a CNN interview, Trump stepped up his attacks on U.S. District Judge Gonzalo Curiel, the son of Mexican immigrants and the presiding judge in lawsuits alleging fraud against Trump University, the New York businessman's defunct real estate training school. Trump suggested that Curiel's Mexican heritage was influencing the judge's view of the case because Trump has campaigned on building a wall along the U.S. border with Mexico to stop illegal immigration. “He’s proud of his heritage,” Trump said. “He’s a Mexican. We’re building a wall between here and Mexico. The answer is, he is giving us very unfair rulings, rulings that people can’t even believe. This case should have ended years ago on summary judgment,” Trump said. A week ago the judge unsealed documents related to the case. Comments from the two top elected U.S. Republicans, House of Representatives Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, reflected continuing worries among establishment Republicans about Trump. Ryan, who endorsed Trump on Thursday, said Trump's comments about the judge were “out of left field.” “He clearly says and does things I don’t agree with.”

title: Trump Caught Telling A Huge Lie About His Shady Foundation
text: Donald Trump is still using his Twitter account to push big, ridiculous lies about his troubled personal foundation, the Donald J. Trump Foundation. Even after winning the presidential election, Trump apparently just can't let the issue go, since it keeps generating negative headlines for him. In a tweet, Trump claimed that 100% of the money donated to the foundation goes to wonderful charities, but as the Huffington Post reports, that is a total lie about how the foundation has operated over the years. The Donald J. Trump Foundation, set up in 1987, admitted to the Internal Revenue Service just last year that it engaged in self-dealing, a banned practice in which a nonprofit leader uses an organization's money to benefit his or her own interests. According to a Washington Post report earlier this month, the foundation's 2015 tax filings confirmed that it had transferred income or assets to a disqualified person that year (in this case, a disqualified person could be Trump himself or a member of his family or business) and had done similar things in previous years. While the media obsessed over the optics and right-wing innuendo about the Clinton Foundation (much of that smear bankrolled by the head of Breitbart, by the way), Trump's foundation escaped much of the same scrutiny despite its admittedly illegal behavior. On top of that, the Trump Foundation gave money to a political group tied to Florida attorney general Pam Bondi, who dropped a probe of Trump University at the same time. The IRS fined the foundation over that. He also used the foundation as a slush fund to settle multiple lawsuits filed against him personally, instead of paying out of his own bank accounts.
